title: How do party gatekeepers and primaries decide who reaches the ballot?
text: It is unknown how parties and voters actually screen candidates, and whether gatekeepers keep women, immigrants and able outsiders off the ballot through discrimination, rent protection or lack of contact. Theory covers how incentives shape selection (Besley 2005) and primary and list-position studies are growing (Galasso and Nannicini 2011, Casey et al. 2021, Casas-Arce and Sáiz 2015, Dancygier et al. 2020), but primaries outside the US and party-internal rules remain thinly studied.
why: Gatekeepers' choices and the pool of aspirants are not observed, and the adoption of primaries and list rules is itself endogenous, so researchers see only the winners of a selection process they cannot observe.

title: What makes people run for office, and can reforms widen the pool?
text: It is unknown what drives the decision to run (motives, costs, family and network ties) and whether competition, training or lower entry barriers improve the candidate pool rather than only the electability of those already willing. Citizen-candidate models under plurality and runoff rules (Besley and Coate 1997, Osborne and Slivinski 1996) and first training and primary interventions (Dal Bó et al. 2024, Casey et al. 2021) exist, but data seldom cover non-politicians, losing candidates or politicians' parents (Thompson et al. 2019).
why: The pool of would-be candidates, including non-runners and losers, is rarely observed, models stop at plurality and runoff rules with exogenous parties and no campaign information, and credible variation in entry costs is scarce.

title: Do pay and returns to office select honest types or rent-seekers?
text: It is unknown whether higher pay, non-financial rewards such as prestige or civic duty, and the rents of office draw in honest and competent people or mainly rent-seekers, and whether better selection and better incentives complement each other. The field has salary evidence on legislator performance (Ferraz and Finan 2010), a pay-and-selection model (Besley 2004) and asset-disclosure evidence of a winner's premium that rises with state corruption (Fisman et al. 2014), but little on honesty, which politicians can mimic.
why: Pay is endogenous to the type it attracts, honest types are hard to tell from mimics, and adverse selection and moral hazard generate the same observed premium.

title: Do competent or honest politicians deliver better policy, and how?
text: It is unknown whether politicians' competence, honesty and valence change policy and government quality, through the policies chosen or how they are implemented, and whether selecting for competence costs social representativeness. Leaders matter for some outcomes, mainly monetary policy and growth (Jones and Olken 2005), and democracies and quotas change who is selected (Besley and Reynal-Querol 2011, Besley et al. 2017), but whether better-selected politicians perform better is open and the Swedish competence gain had faded by 2014.
why: Competence, honesty and education come bundled and are hard to measure, close-election designs cannot isolate one trait without post-treatment bias, and quota instruments exist only in a few places.

title: Do quota effects persist and hold for other designs and countries?
text: It is unknown whether quota effects persist beyond a few electoral cycles, whether permanent reservation entrenches new monopolies, and which designs (reserved seats, zip lists, rules restricting cross-gender competition) work outside Indian village councils. Randomised and close-election studies, mostly in India, Brazil, Sweden and Spain, give credible estimates (Chattopadhyay and Duflo 2004, Brollo and Troiano 2016, O'Brien and Rickne 2016, Bagues and Campa 2020), but they repeatedly stop at one city, one design or three electoral cycles.
why: Identification relies on a rule that creates as-good-as-random variation, usually in one country with a short panel, so quota type, scale and horizon are confounded with place.

title: Do quotas raise targeted groups' welfare, and through which link?
text: It is unknown through which links descriptive representation reaches the welfare of the targeted group (targeted spending, party control over renomination, legislators' voice, household take-up) and whether outcomes beneficiaries value actually improve. Reserved seats can shift spending towards the targeted group (Pande 2003) while reserved-seat politicians may still not redistribute (Jensenius 2015), but the chain from policy adoption to child health, mortality or tribal welfare is only partly traced (Rustagi and Akter 2022, Gulzar et al. 2023).
why: Welfare outcomes arrive years after adoption and need linked household-level data, survival and migration confound child-health comparisons, and party constraints on reserved-seat politicians are documented mostly through interviews rather than tested.

title: How do dynasties persist and what do they cost in governance?
text: It is unknown through which channels (name recognition, contacts, family networks, favoured access to jobs) dynasties and political connections perpetuate themselves, and what they cost in policy-making, service delivery and rents outside the few countries studied. Dynastic self-perpetuation in the US Congress (Dal Bó et al. 2008), relatives' rents in Sweden (Folke et al. 2017) and the electoral weight of family networks (Cruz et al. 2017) are documented, but analyses of why dynasties arise are well ahead of analyses of what they do.
why: Consequences are hard to separate from the selection of family members into politics, records of relatives' careers and local service delivery are rarely linked, and the settings studied may not carry over to less transparent institutions.

title: How can vote buying be measured credibly beyond case studies?
text: It is unknown how widespread vote buying and clientelist linkages are beyond documented cases, because no valid cross-national measure exists that separates vote buying, turnout buying and double persuasion. The field relies on surveys, list experiments and single-country studies (Vicente 2013, González-Ocantos et al. 2011, Wantchekon 2003, Bobonis et al. 2025), whose authors flag conformity and social-desirability bias, obfuscation by the actors themselves and context dependence.
why: Respondents and political actors have reasons to hide the exchange, the boundary between vote buying, turnout buying and persuasion is blurred in practice, and survey answers are biased by conformity and social desirability.

title: How do parties motivate, monitor and choose brokers and targets?
text: It is unknown what motivates political brokers, which monitoring mechanisms besides electoral returns let parties discipline them, how parties choose among brokers (unions, priests, ethnic or traditional leaders) and whom they target, including when rival machines compete. Case-based and experimental evidence covers specific brokers and targeting rules, such as Mexican public-sector unions (Larreguy et al. 2016, 2017) and Argentine machines (Stokes 2005), but the conditions behind variation across localities and parties are little understood.
why: Brokers and their contracts are hidden, parties rarely face comparable rivals or monitoring technologies within one setting, and most evidence comes from a few country cases.

title: Why do voters comply with clientelism: reciprocity, fear, monitoring?
text: It is unknown what makes voters honour clientelist exchanges, whether reciprocity, an individual propensity to vote, fear of losing an entitlement, deference to local authorities or the risk of being monitored, and which voters are cheapest to bind. Brokers are known to target reciprocal individuals (Finan and Schechter 2012) and responses to clientelist appeals differ across voters, including by sex (Wantchekon 2003), but the channels are rarely separated and other-regarding preferences challenge the assumptions of standard voting models.
why: Reciprocity, loss aversion, fear and monitoring produce the same observed compliance in most designs, and good individual-level measures of propensity to vote or psychological traits are missing.

title: What does patronage cost in welfare, and when does it deliver?
text: It is unknown what patronage and vote buying cost in welfare terms (incentive, selection and match effects, an oversized bureaucracy, worse service delivery) and when patronage ties deliver services rather than extract rents, for instance only in low-capacity settings. Some costs of patronage hiring are quantified (Colonnelli et al. 2020, Xu 2018) and the same governance resources are shown to serve delivery or extraction (Toral 2023), while robust evidence linking neopatrimonial politics to poor economic outcomes in Africa is still missing (Mkandawire 2015).
why: Almost every comparison municipality or bureaucracy also has patronage, so counterfactuals are missing, and selection, incentive and match effects are hard to separate in one design.

title: What durably weakens clientelism: insurance, cash or information?
text: It is unknown whether insurance, cash transfers, information or hiring reform make citizens abandon clientelist ties altogether, through which channel, and whether effects last once programmes scale, repeat or leave Brazil and Uganda. Experiments show that insurance, anti-corruption information and one-off grants shift political behaviour in the short run (Bobonis et al. 2022, 2025, Blattman et al. 2018) and observational work covers civil-service reform and programmatic transitions (Folke et al. 2011, Brierley 2020, Stokes et al. 2013), but all rest on few settings and short horizons.
why: The treatments are one-off experiments or reforms with non-random timing, so durability, scale effects and the channel (misattribution, group socialisation, financial independence) cannot be separated with the evidence at hand.

title: Do incumbents mix fraud, violence and vote buying, and does it pay?
text: It is unknown how incumbents jointly choose among vote buying, miscounting and violence, which settings (ethnic allegiances, resources, term limits, moderate insecurity) favour each, and whether leaders who use election violence actually stay in power. Formal models of illicit strategies and of why insecure rulers hold elections exist (Collier and Vicente 2011, 2013, Little 2012), as does cross-national work on election violence and enfranchisement (Hafner-Burton et al. 2013, Lacroix 2022), but tests are scarce and the strategies are usually studied one at a time.
why: Datasets covering violence, miscounting and vote buying together are lacking, ex post outcomes such as regime duration are confounded when proxies like polls or riots are used, and actors hide the manipulation.

title: Do observers, audits and open data curb political manipulation?
text: It is unknown whether domestic or foreign observers, election-timed audits, image-based tally audits, wider polling-station access and public inspection data deter fraud and the political manipulation of service delivery, and when those in power act on the information. Field experiments on monitoring, audits and inspection data exist (Callen and Long 2015, Brollo et al. 2019, Callen et al. 2023, Larreguy et al. 2016), but the authors ask whether effects are sustainable, whether evidence alone changes delivery where power is concentrated, and what the net effect is across contexts.
why: Most monitoring evidence comes from single interventions in one setting, politicians object to or ignore the data when it threatens them, and forensic tools for auditing other elections are still being built.

title: How can corruption be measured objectively and comparably?
text: It is unknown how to measure corruption objectively and comparably (payment processes, price effects on users, hypothetical tax yield, hidden cheating, political connectedness) when perceptions and victim surveys are systematically biased. Micro studies observe corrupt payments or their direct consequences in one sector or country at a time (Olken and Barron 2009, Bertrand et al. 2007) and cross-country work uses perception indices (Treisman 2000), but the authors call for objective measures that travel across sectors, countries and time.
why: Corruption is illegal and hidden, perceptions are biased, direct observation exists only for narrow settings, and bribe, demand and firm productivity data are rarely matched.

title: Does anti-corruption policy work in equilibrium and in the long run?
text: It is unknown whether audits, monitoring, transparency and enforcement reduce corruption net of substitution to other forms, price responses by remaining bribe takers, entry of criminal organisations and general-equilibrium spillovers, and whether effects last once agents learn or norms habituate. Experimental and quasi-experimental evidence exists on audits, monitoring and information (Olken 2007, Reinikka and Svensson 2004), but the authors repeatedly note one-shot settings, partial-equilibrium estimates and thin evidence on long-run or system-wide effects (Olken and Pande 2012, Avis et al. 2018).
why: Audit and monitoring experiments run once, in one place and over short horizons, so substitution, rotation and equilibrium responses cannot be observed without repeated or system-wide designs.

title: What does corruption cost beyond theft, and who bears it?
text: It is unknown what corruption and connections cost beyond the resources stolen (distorted allocation of inputs, hiring and credit, forgone quality in public contracts, effects on trade) and who bears the losses across income groups. Firm-level effects (Colonnelli and Prem 2021) and credit misallocation inside an elite network (Haselmann et al. 2018) have been estimated, but the authors say causal evidence on social costs is lacking and welfare estimates need data matching bribes to demand and firms to productivity (Fisman and Wang 2015, Sequeira and Djankov 2014).
why: The evidence is observational, bribes are rarely matched to demand and firms to productivity, and second-best theory cautions against reading misallocation as a welfare loss.

title: How do connections create firm value, and what limits extraction?
text: It is unknown through which channels (procurement, credit, regulation, policy information) political connections raise firm value, what alternative rent-extraction routes open when one closes, and why firms deal with government through personal ties rather than formal mechanisms. Connection premia and credit misallocation have been measured in several countries (Fisman 2001, Khwaja and Mian 2005, Cingano and Pinotti 2013, Haselmann et al. 2018), but mechanisms remain largely unexplored, connectedness is hard to define where power is decentralised, and results may not carry beyond the single club, country or episode studied.
why: Connectedness is hard to define and observe when power is decentralised and ties shift, and channels are bundled together in firm-level outcomes so credit, regulation and procurement effects cannot be separated.

title: Why does corruption persist in some places and how do others exit?
text: It is unknown what makes corruption higher in one place than another (institutions, culture, development, electoral discipline, expected future rents) and how places exit high-corruption equilibria, including why governments tolerate petty bribery and why rich-country health bureaucracies are clean. Cross-country regressions (Treisman 2000, Mauro 1995), models of misgovernance (Banerjee 1997) and evidence that electoral accountability limits local corruption (Ferraz and Finan 2007) exist, but reverse causality from poverty to institutions remains and the root causes are poorly understood.
why: Cross-country corruption data are perception-based and endogenous to income and institutions, and settings with exogenous variation in culture or institutions are rare, so reverse causality and multiple equilibria cannot be separated.

title: Does competition limit corruption risk in discretionary procurement?
text: It is unknown through which mechanisms procurement discretion, bidder competition and audit design drive corruption and waste, including for one-of-a-kind goods that make up much of public purchasing, and whether moving from auctions to direct contracts raises prices. Correlations between discretion, competition and corruption risk (Decarolis et al. 2024), a split of waste into active and passive components (Bandiera et al. 2009) and contract reallocation to connected firms (Brugués et al. 2024) are documented, but causal designs, price data beyond a few countries and evidence on unofficial arrangements are missing.
why: Comparable price data exist only for standardised goods in a few settings, quality shading and unofficial arrangements are unobserved, and discretion is chosen endogenously by agencies and officials.

title: How are bribes and extortion priced, centralised and enforced?
text: It is unknown what lets corrupt officials and gangs coordinate and centralise collection, set prices and sustain complex illegal arrangements, what intermediaries do to price discrimination and access, and how users and demand respond to the price of bribes. Bribe payments on trucking routes (Olken and Barron 2009), agent-mediated licensing (Bertrand et al. 2007) and gang extortion (Brown et al. 2024) have been observed directly, but the authors call for micro data on payment processes and note that price elasticities and the effect of limiting bribe takers have to be inferred.
why: Bribes are paid in secret, so prices, elasticities and the role of intermediaries are rarely observed outside a few hand-collected settings, and the counterfactual for limiting bribe takers is missing.

title: What builds state capacity, and what do investments in it return?
text: It is unknown which forces causally build legal and fiscal capacity (ethnic division, instability, conflict, resource rents, coalitions, legitimacy), why capacity-raising reform is not adopted when models say it should be, how societies exit weak-capacity and clientelism traps, and what specific capacity investments return once measured and scaled. Theory on investment in state capacity is rich (Besley and Persson 2009, 2010, 2011) and correlational evidence links capacity, centralisation and growth (Dincecco and Katz 2014), but the authors stress that more territory is unexplored than settled and that causal and individual-level evidence is thin.
why: State capacity moves slowly, is endogenous to the conflict, income and institutions it is meant to explain, and is measured mainly at the country level or by retrospective performance, so causal designs and individual-level evidence are rare.

title: How to raise tax compliance where third-party information is missing?
text: It is unknown which levers raise tax compliance where informality and weak capacity leave no third-party information (enforcement, consumer rewards, collector incentives, taxpayer loans, legitimacy), how they interact, and whether effects survive beyond two years or scale without pushing firms into informality. Strong experimental evidence exists for single levers, such as performance pay for tax collectors (Khan et al. 2015), consumer rewards (Naritomi 2019) and third-party enforcement (Kleven et al. 2016), but the authors call for long-run cost-effectiveness comparisons and direct tests of when each lever works.
why: Each study evaluates one lever in one setting over a short horizon, informality and taxpayers' strategic responses are hard to observe, and credible variation in enforcement capacity is rare.

title: Do pay, exams and screening select public workers who perform better?
text: It is unknown whether pay, performance pay, exams and dishonesty screens change who selects into public jobs along ability, honesty and prosociality, whether recruits perform better once hired, and how sorting evolves in the long run. Experiments and sorting studies show that wages and career incentives shape applicant pools (Dal Bó et al. 2013, Ashraf et al. 2020) and that dishonest people sort into public jobs (Hanna and Wang 2017), but performance after hiring, whether performance pay attracts abler teachers (Muralidharan and Sundararaman 2011) and the distributional effects of exams are unobserved.
why: Long-run sorting cannot be observed in an experimental sample, performance data on those hired are rarely linked to recruitment arms, and corruption-proneness is hard to measure before entry.

title: Which management practices and incentives raise public-sector output?
text: It is unknown which management practices, assignment rules, mission framing and incentive allocations across the layers of a hierarchy raise public-sector output, which of them is the active ingredient, and why managers do not already adopt cheap fixes such as emphasising the mission. Managers matter for productivity (Fenizia 2022), promotion incentives affect worker output (Deserranno et al. 2025) and mission matters (Khan 2025, Besley and Ghatak 2005), but the authors ask whether this carries to other organisations, larger teams, unclear missions and delegation to line managers.
why: Management, mission and hierarchy design are bundled in real organisations, most studies randomise one practice in one agency, and results from researcher-run programmes may not survive delegation to line managers.

title: Does bureaucratic autonomy raise delivery without political will?
text: It is unknown whether insulating bureaucrats and their overseers from politicians raises delivery when political will is weak, why bureaucracies nonetheless rely on costly rules rather than autonomy, and how patronage and multiple principals shape what civil servants, auditors and regulators do. Civil-service reform and rules change performance and politicians' policy choices (Aneja and Xu 2024, Ujhelyi 2014), multiple principals weaken implementation (Gulzar and Pasquale 2016) and auditors can be captured (Hidalgo et al. 2016, Vannutelli 2022), but experiments that manipulate autonomy and remedies for capture are missing.
why: Autonomy, political will and patronage are endogenous to one another and rarely manipulated, so field experiments that randomise autonomy are scarce and political constraints are documented mostly through cases and correlations.

title: Which accountability reforms last, and which component does the work?
text: It is unknown which component of monitoring, incentive and participation reforms in frontline services does the work (information or participation, pay or daily monitoring, a single audit element), whether effects persist beyond two years once workers adapt or collude, and how to cut absence at scale. Randomised evidence shows community monitoring, attendance incentives and audit reforms improve delivery in the short run (Björkman and Svensson 2009, Duflo et al. 2012, 2013), but long-term effects, mechanisms and cross-sector externalities are untested, and a health mobilisation that worked in Uganda had an education counterpart that did not (Banerjee et al. 2010).
why: Most evaluations follow treated units for two years or less, interventions bundle several components, and adaptation by workers and officials (collusion, changes in who joins) appears only over longer horizons.

title: Does decentralising or splitting jurisdictions improve provision?
text: It is unknown whether decentralisation, jurisdiction splitting and smaller polities improve the level and quality of public goods, growth and democracy relative to centralised provision, and what they cost in weaker monitoring, local capture, limits to local taxation and lower politician quality. Theory and surveys cover capture, yardstick competition and the fiscal limits of local government (Bardhan and Mookherjee 2000, Gadenne and Singhal 2014) and early evidence exists on district and county splits (Grossman and Lewis 2014, Lipscomb and Mobarak 2016), but direct comparisons with centralised provision are rare and the channels largely untested.
why: Decentralisation is adopted for reasons correlated with outcomes, direct centralised counterfactuals are rare, and the costs of splitting (monitoring, corruption, politician quality) lack data.
